items.description_html:
Last 5 years would have humbled a lot of investors

There was a time when the playbook looked simple:
- Buy a blue chip
- Hold it forever
- Forget about quarterly numbers
- Expect 20% CAGR

The era of lazy investing is being seriously challenged

Businesses, competitive advantages & industry structures are changing faster than ever

Some of the strongest businesses, established market leaders & supposedly recession proof sectors have delivered negligible or even negative returns

Look at how many supposedly strong narratives have been shaken:

1. FMCG : Cash rich businesses, recession resistant demand, predictable earnings & whatnot!

When REV growth remains in single digits for years, even exceptional ROCE & strong cash generation cannot justify premium valuations indefinitely

A company cannot keep trading at 50-60x P/E forever without meaningful earnings growth

Eventually, valuations have to catch up with the underlying growth reality!

For years, the biggest moat for the sector was distribution

Thousands of distributors + lakhs of retail outlets made it extremely difficult for a new brand to compete with established FMCG giants

Quick Commerce gives a new brand access to consumers almost instantly

D2C brands can build awareness online, launch nationally & reach customers without spending decades building physical distribution

The incumbents are still extremely strong businesses, but distribution alone is no longer the moat it once was

2. IT Services : The Traditional Growth Model Is Under Pressure

For decades, Indian IT companies benefited from global outsourcing & labour cost arbitrage

More global outsourcing → More employees → More REV → More profits

But AI is potentially changing the economics of the entire industry

The traditional headcount led growth model is being challenged, while discretionary spending remains weak

The old narrative cannot simply be extrapolated

3. Paints : Even Strong Entry Barriers Can Be Challenged

The paints industry was once considered one of the strongest consumer franchises

Distribution + dealer relationships + brand + tinting machines created enormous entry barriers

Then a large new player entered with massive capacity, aggressive dealer expansion & pricing

Suddenly an industry believed to have almost impenetrable barriers had to deal with a completely new competitive environment

Again, the businesses didn't suddenly become bad

The competitive structure changed

And these are just a few examples!

A company that was a market leader 5 years ago may still be a market leader today, but its growth prospects, competitive advantages & valuations could be completely different

You have to do the hard work!

Track quarterly results, management commentary, competitive intensity, market share & changing industry dynamics

Most importantly, keep questioning your original investment thesis.

items.description_html:
RT ValueEquity
Laurus Labs and Aarvik Therapeutics , lets see what is the interesting work that goes on at Aarvik ,

Aarvik has very interesting and science backed proprietary MUTTA™ platform and next-generation Antibody-Drug Conjugate (ADC) technology , that separates their technology in ADC from the original GEN1 and Gen2 ADC's , they also have an Aqualink platform Aarvik along with Arrivent Biopharma will present AV-P138-ADC , a novel ADC , for treatment of Ovarian and Endometrial cancers

ARR002 , a novel site specific conjugated mechanism , ( this was discovered by Aarvik in partnership with Arrivent , who subsequently globally licensed the molecule for global development

Laurus has invested in them in the seed 2 stage , for laurus this is a deep capability investment that enables them to gain and learn these high science ADC technology that can given them a significant edge in their own product development and learnings as well Now why this is important , and I write about this even after being a shareholder for 4 years , is how actively management keep investing and broadening the capability depth , when laurus was a pure ARV play very few could have visualised them going into such high precision ADC tech and focusing on large modalities with capacity first approach

This might be bit technical , but just something I found very interesting reading about Aarvik

items.title: RT Prasanna Viswanathan: “Bittu Tabahi aka Surendra Singh, a 20-year-old BSc student from Biaora in Madhya Pradesh’s Rajgarh district, In January he...
items.description_html:
RT Prasanna Viswanathan
“Bittu Tabahi aka Surendra Singh, a 20-year-old BSc student from Biaora in Madhya Pradesh’s Rajgarh district,

In January he began cleaning a choked stretch of the Ajnar river on his own, working without gloves, protective gear, machinery or a municipal crew.

Over 7 months he removed plastic, sludge, algae and solid waste by hand. Videos of the cleanup went viral. MP CM Mohan Yadav called him to Bhopal and assured him of government support.

About a month after the appreicated cleanup, the river had filled with garbage again. Bittu was trolled online by usual scummies and nearly gave up. But he chose to continue. Rajgarh district administration has since honoured him and pledged support, which gives what began as a one-man effort a chance of institutional backing.

One person can perform inspirational act but keeping it clean depends on regular waste collection, public bins, drainage, enforcement, and residents taking responsibility for the river. Hopefully administration will now do justice to Bittu’s inspiring effort by putting systems in place on the ground. @timesofindia

BREAKING: The S&P Global US Manufacturing PMI index rose +0.1 point in October, to 56.0, its highest level since May 2022.

This exceeded expectations of a -0.4 point decline.

The improvement was particularly driven by job growth, which rose to its strongest level since March 2012.

Meanwhile, the Services PMI index fell -0.9 points, to 57.9, its 2nd-highest level in 4 years.

This brought the Composite PMI index down -0.8 points, to 57.6, also its 2nd-highest in 4 years.

Despite the slight decline, these readings point to GDP growth of +5.0% at an annualized rate in Q4 2026, following projected growth of +4.0% in Q3 2026.

US economic growth is booming amid the AI Revolution.

items.title: US equity market breadth is rapidly improving: The proportion of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 50-day moving average surged +5 percentage points ...
items.description_html:
US equity market breadth is rapidly improving:

The proportion of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 50-day moving average surged +5 percentage points on Friday, to 61%, the highest reading since mid-August.

Since the October 1st intraday low, this figure has more than tripled.

Additionally, the proportion of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 200-day moving average rose +3 percentage points on Friday, to 57%, the most since September 9th.

Over the last 3 weeks, this figure has risen +17 percentage points.

This comes despite the S&P 500 remaining roughly unchanged over the same period.

This also ranks among the 3 sharpest improvements in market breadth over the last 3 years.

On Thursday alone, 335 S&P 500 stocks finished higher, despite the index declining -1.2% on that day.

The market is strengthening beneath the surface.

#Lupin crossed ₹2500 crore of PAT in FY17. It took eight years to get back above it.

In 2015, the market was paying ~40x earnings.

When the valuation is that high, “profits will grow” isn’t an assumption. It is the investment thesis.

Profits did grow. Just too late. The stock is still below its 2015 level.

Lupin is a case study for today’s “hot” themes: CDMO, aerospace, AI/semiconductors, defence.

Great stories. High multiples. Profits that have to arrive on time.

History often rhymes.

Meanwhile, speculative investors, including hedge funds and commodity trading advisers (CTAs), sold -$2.2 billion in silver futures over the 3 weeks ending October 13th.

As a result, their net long positioning is down to just +$1.7 billion, the lowest in at least 2 years.

For perspective, this metric stood at +$8.5 billion in December 2025.

Investors are extremely bearish on silver.

Health insurance has never been more expensive.

items.title: Rajeev Jain shared some interesting insights on Gold Loans during Bajaj Finance's Q2FY27 concall! Bajaj Finance has already built a 24,000 Cr Gold Loa...
items.description_html:
Rajeev Jain shared some interesting insights on Gold Loans during Bajaj Finance's Q2FY27 concall!

Bajaj Finance has already built a 24,000 Cr Gold Loan book (+105% YoY)

It is now among the top 5 Gold Loan lenders in the NBFC sector

- Gold Loans should be a “profit builder”, not an “AUM builder”

- Bajaj experimented with short tenure Gold Loans, but these created unnecessary technical delinquencies when customers missed maturity dates

- 1,047 Cr of Gold Loans moved into Stage 2 during the quarter largely because of this structure

- Management stopped these short tenure schemes from August itself

- 550 Cr had already moved back to Stage 1 by the time of the concall

- Company now prefers longer 9-12 month tenures while still allowing customers to repay earlier

- 99% of Gold Loan customers currently use bullet repayment

- Management does not want to build an auction driven Gold Loan franchise

- It is willing to accept slower AUM growth rather than push higher LTVs or products that could unnecessarily stress customers

- Average ticket size remains ~2.4-2.5 lakh with LTV around 75%, including interest

Some excellent insights into the nuances of the Gold Loan business!

items.title: RT Persistence Capital: Here's a simple framework that helped us navigate the last few years well. During euphoric times, shorten your time horizon. T...
items.description_html:
RT Persistence Capital
Here's a simple framework that helped us navigate the last few years well.

During euphoric times, shorten your time horizon. This'll reduce the likelihood of overpaying and permanent loss of capital.

During despondent times, lengthen your time horizon. Portfolio companies may look super cheap in the out years and this'll increase the likelihood that you buy the dip.

Always remember, nothing is certain. The above framework is a necessary but not sufficient condition to generating strong absolute / relative returns over the long term.

items.title: EAAA India Alternatives raises ~Rs 360 crore from Anchor Investors, includes Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global and global asset manager Schrode...
items.description_html:
EAAA India Alternatives raises ~Rs 360 crore from Anchor Investors, includes Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global and global asset manager Schroders

EAAA India Alternatives Limited (“EAAA”), which is one of the Leading Alternatives platforms in India with over 17 years of experience of managing Long Term Patient capital, has successfully raised ~ ₹ 360 crores from anchor investors today, ahead of its initial public offering that opens for public subscription on October 26, 2026.

Strong Response from Anchor Investors-----

As per the data submitted with the exchanges, all the Top 5 Mutual Funds in India participated in the Anchor book namely HDFC MF, ICICI Prudential MF, SBI MF, Nippon MF & Kotak MF. A total of 10 mutual funds invested accounting for 61% of the anchor book, with others being Bandhan, HSBC, 360 ONE, Abakkus, and Trust Mutual Fund.

Marquee Global Institutional Investors like Government Pension Fund Global one of the World’s Largest Sovereign Wealth Fund managed by Norges Bank Investment Management (with fund value of nearly $2.3 trillion) and Schroders, a Global Asset Manager also participated into the anchor round along with other Long only FIIs.

There was also significant participation from well-known Indian Asset managers like Carnelian, 360 ONE, Unifi and Nuvama.

The IPO opens on Monday for subscription to Public.

The robust anchor investor demand from Top Mutual Funds & marquee Global Institutions reflects their confidence in the long-term growth of alternatives industry in India where EAAA is uniquely positioned to tap this opportunity.

Axis Capital, Jefferies, Motilal Oswal and Nuvama are the Book Running Lead Managers, and Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas, Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas and LinkLaters are the legal counsels associated with this Issue.

IPO Details
The Issue Size is ₹ 1,200.00 crore. The Issue will open on October 26, 2026 for subscription and close on October 28, 2026.

Investors can bid for a minimum of 9 Equity Shares and in multiples of 9 Equity Shares thereafter.

items.description_html:
Modi Says Buy Less Gold. Imports Crash 81%. Coincidence?

In May, PM Modi urged Indians to avoid unnecessary gold purchases. In September, he repeated the appeal.

Meanwhile, gold import duties jumped from 6% to 15%.

September imports collapsed to just $1.8 billion down 81% YoY.

High prices, domestic recycling and government policy are all potentially reshaping demand.

But here's the bigger question: Is Modi's appeal actually changing India's gold-buying behaviour, or are economics doing the heavy lifting?

For India, the implications extend beyond jewellery to the trade deficit, forex reserves and rupee.

items.title: Shakti pumps after doing peak margins of 24% is now at margins of 8.6% and here's why? In a B2G business the user and the payer are different people. ...
items.description_html:
Shakti pumps after doing peak margins of 24% is now at margins of 8.6% and here's why?

In a B2G business the user and the payer are different people. When the farmer pays ~10% and the government pays the rest, demand is almost infinite, so TAM tells you nothing. Shakti’s deck shows a 5.5 lakh Cr TAM, while PM-KUSUM’s actual outlay was 34,422 Cr, about 6% of it. Even the rumoured ~50,000 Cr outlay for PM-KUSUM 2.0 takes you to about 9%.

So demand in such businesses is mostly not a problem as an investor one has to solve for rather the problem to solve for in most cases is the government.

The government holds three pens here. The Price pen set one rate contract (~2.36 lakh per pump in Maharashtra, the same for every vendor)

The Calendar pen let PM-KUSUM phase 1 sunset with 2.0 still not at Cabinet, and Shakti’s order book fell from ~₹2,100 Cr to ₹751 Cr in eight months

The Cheque pen routes money through Centre, state, nodal agency and a verification desk before it reaches you.

And players like Shakti hold only one pen i.e. execution.

The result is in the numbers. From FY24 to H1 FY27, Shakti reported ~898 Cr of PAT but negative 254 Cr of operating cash. FY25, its best year at 24% EBITDA margin, converted just 5% of profit into cash. QIPs and bank lines funded the gap

And this wasn’t Shakti-specific. Oswal’s receivable days went from 111 to 229, and asset-light GK Energy converted only ~26% of FY26 profit into cash.

On top of it they have been badly hurt by rising raw material inflation + higher logistics costs for export orders with lower realisations with revised prices. Also with this ALMM II compliant module prices are also up 15-20% which might also be hurting them

And their finance cost is rising with rising working capital financing.

Government money rarely defaults. The real risk is duration: how long you wait, and the interest, dilution and forgone growth you pay while waiting.

So when you look at any B2G business ask these questions to yourself -

1) Who pays?
2) Who sets the price?
3) Where is the scheme in its cycle? A scheme’s sunset is when the order book shrinks and receivables swell at the same time.
4) What is cumulative PAT vs cumulative CFO over three years?
5) Who is funding the gap?

Disclaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.description_html:
BREAKING: The total value of the US stock market has surged to 350% of the US M2 money supply, the highest level since the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble.

Since the 2022 bear market, this ratio has surged +170 percentage points.

Over this period, the S&P 500 has rallied +118%, while M2 has risen +9%.

In other words, the stock market's gain has outpaced the money supply growth by 13x.

The last time equity market growth exceeded M2 growth by a larger amount was from 1995 to 1999.

Asset owners are winning.

items.title: Investors are betting on more upside in US Treasuries. The extra cost investors are willing to pay for call options on longer-dated Treasuries relativ...
items.description_html:
Investors are betting on more upside in US Treasuries.

The extra cost investors are willing to pay for call options on longer-dated Treasuries relative to puts is up to ~50 basis points, the highest since March 2025.

This marks a sharp reversal from a 250-basis-point premium for puts over calls in late September.

This suggests investors are increasingly betting on further gains in Treasury prices.

Furthermore, one options trade is targeting a drop in the 10Y Note Yield to ~4.60% within a month, involving ~65,000 contracts and costing ~$7 million in premium.

This comes as the 10Y Note Yield has declined below 5.00% for the first time since September 23rd, now down -40 basis points from the October 7th peak.

The bond market is seeing massive swings in price and sentiment.

items.title: I read something about Airbus and Air India 1980-1990 - Air India (Indian Airlines that merged with Air India) placed an order for 31 airbus A320 seri...
items.description_html:
I read something about Airbus and Air India

1980-1990 - Air India (Indian Airlines that merged with Air India) placed an order for 31 airbus A320 series of aircraft and airbus designed a custom version for them

Now what was custom?

The landing gear, aircrafts of that size come with two wheels on both its landing gear but Air India demanded a version that had 4 wheels on each landing gear. this required expensive modification to the aircraft and retesting and certification of the variant

Question is why such requirement?

Air India was the largest airline operator in India and used to operate flights even at remote airports which didn’t have the best quality of runway. The runways in many of these airports were bumpy so other airlines operated propeller engined aircraft’s which were smaller. (primary issue was inadequate runway pavement strength)

Air India wanted to use larger aircraft’s and thus this requirement. The last of these aircraft’s were retired in 2019!

France's (A+/Negative) fiscal and debt metrics remain under pressure, as fiscal slippages have kept the debt trajectory elevated. With public debt continuing to exceed medium-term targets and recent budget measures offering only a modest reduction in the fiscal deficit, investor concerns have intensified amid rising debt-servicing costs, weak growth prospects and expectations of continued debt accumulation.
The widening of French sovereign spreads highlights the extent to which fiscal strain and policy uncertainty are weighing on market confidence. Although France retains important credit strengths, including strong institutions, a large and diversified economy and deep capital markets, concerns over fiscal sustainability, policy uncertainty and reform execution continue to challenge the government's ability to place debt on a durable downward trajectory.

AI can write a report, summarise a study and generate content in seconds. But how do we know if the information it gives us is correct?

Knowing how to use AI is one thing. Knowing when to question its answers, verify the facts, make sense of data and communicate what we find is just as important.

These are skills that researchers, journalists, communicators and development professionals need today.

items.title: Zetwerk is among the first venture backed, manufacturing-focused tech platforms from India’s startup ecosystem to go public. Kae Capital (along with ...
items.description_html:
Zetwerk is among the first venture backed, manufacturing-focused tech platforms from India’s startup ecosystem to go public.

Kae Capital (along with affiliate Kalysta Capital) is the standout winner. It invested at an average cost of just Rs 3.94 a share.

At Zetwerk’s Rs 151 IPO price, that translates into a 38x return.

It has sold shares worth over Rs 253 crore, and will collectively hold 3.33% stake worth Rs 868 crore.

Other early investors have also done well.

Peak XV Partners: Making about 24x return. Sold shares worth Rs 266 crore and retaining a 7.1% stake worth ~Rs 1,849 crore.

Peak holds another 2.4% stake through late stage funds, and will make about 3x.

Accel India: Making 19x return, selling Rs 181 crore and retaining 6.2% stake worth Rs 1,611 crore.

Lightspeed India: About 11x return, selling Rs 175 crore and retaining 2.7% stake worth Rs 693 crore.

Lightspeed later funds hold 4.5% stake, and will make about 3x.

But the biggest institutional shareholder is taking a very different approach.

Greenoaks is not selling a single share in the IPO.

Across four entities, it owns nearly 20% pre-IPO, making it Zetwerk’s largest shareholder.

After dilution, Greenoaks will still own about 17.5%, worth roughly Rs 4,557 crore at the IPO price.


The Arc: 🚨 Zetwerk was listed on Friday, with its share price opening at a 5% premium to IPO price of Rs 151 before slipping into red.

Current market cap stands at Rs 24,900 crore.

The Rs 5,012 crore IPO was subscribed 3x earlier this week.

items.description_html:
RT Chandra R. Srikanth
🚨 Exclusive: WestBridge Capital's relationship with one of its key limited partners (LPs), Princeton University, has come under strain, with the US university seeking to redeem its investment in the India-focused investment firm over the next few quarters, at least six people familiar with the matter told Moneycontrol.

WestBridge is one of India's most prominent and storied investors in both private and public markets. It has backed more than a dozen unicorns and invested in listed companies across sectors such as IT services, financial services, aviation and healthcare.

Princeton was among the key anchor investors in WestBridge, with the relationship also having a personal dimension through the fund's co-founder and managing director Sumir Chadha, who graduated from Princeton in 1993.

Chadha also served as a trustee on the Princeton University board for a brief period.

WestBridge's own history is closely intertwined with Sequoia Capital India. The firm was founded in 2000 by Sumir Chadha, K.P. Balaraj and Raj Dugar. Dugar left in 2003, while Chadha and Balaraj later brought in Sandeep Singhal and S.K. Jain.

WestBridge merged with Sequoia Capital in 2006 to form Sequoia Capital India. In 2011, Chadha, Balaraj, Singhal and Jain left Sequoia and revived WestBridge as an independent investment firm, with a greater focus on public-market and crossover investments.

WestBridge Capital is also distinctive in that it does not confine itself to early-stage, late-stage, public-market or private-market investing. It invests anywhere between $10 million and $500 million, with an investment horizon of five to 25 years, compared with the five- to seven-year holding period typical of its peers.

Its evergreen fund structure allows it to take a long-term view without being under pressure to exit investments quickly.

items.title: RT Ramesh Srivats: The EDF (Export Declaration Form) rules are now in effect, and it seems like RBI and banks have conspired to create a new hell. Or ...
items.description_html:
RT Ramesh Srivats
The EDF (Export Declaration Form) rules are now in effect, and it seems like RBI and banks have conspired to create a new hell. Or actually 5 hells.

I consult for an American company. Raised October invoice. Received the Inward remittance. And bang! Mail from @HDFC_Bank detailing everything needed before the payment can be processed.

Let me tell you what the 5 hells are:

1. The hell of confusion – RBI clarified last month that the EDF rules do not apply to individuals. But looks like they haven’t told the banks. And CAs also don’t seem to know. There’s no official communication on who is exempt. Last I checked, I was an individual. No company, no LLP. But HDFC still wants me to file the EDF to credit my payment.

2. The hell of complexity – See the attached pic of the form the bank has sent in excel. It has 5 sheets. To be filled and submitted. Some abstruse acronyms like “AD” - no clue what it means. Some fields are mandatory. Some fields are to be filled by the bank. No idea which is what. And it needs a physical signature. Which leads to...

3. The hell of paperwork - They also sent a pdf with a bunch of request letters. I’m supposed to choose the right letter, print, sign, scan and submit. Creating more paper today is incredibly silly. And, I suppose, someone in the bank will have to upload all this somewhere. Reminds me of those hand-filled immigration forms. Pointless.

4. The hell of repetition – At least for me, most of the details are constant. One client, one payment. If it’s a one-time exercise, fine. I’ll grit my teeth and get it done. But no. These details have to be given month after month. Else… no payment will be credited.

5. The hell of unpreparedness – It would have been simple enough for RBI or HDFC to create an online portal for this. With dropdowns, saved formats, contextual help, etc. to at least make this easy. But that would be too convenient, no? So, they’ve chosen to dump the entire burden on the taxpayer.

I have no opinion or understanding of why this is needed. Maybe it is critical information. Okay! But why make the process so confusing and painful?

And poor communication has meant that the banks have just passed on the pain to the exporter, and even CAs can’t help.

Basically RBI & HDFC feel I should consult less, and comply more. Maybe my client will also agree :)

items.title: Same Country. Same Sovereign Risk. But Its 10-Year Bonds Look Expensive While Its 30-Year Bonds Look Cheap. MS's sovereign bond analysis reveals an in...
items.description_html:
Same Country. Same Sovereign Risk. But Its 10-Year Bonds Look Expensive While Its 30-Year Bonds Look Cheap.

MS's sovereign bond analysis reveals an interesting divergence.

Saudi Arabia, Poland, Mexico, Turkey, Romania and Indonesia all show cheap 30Y versus rich 10Y classifications.

Bahrain, Oman and Uruguay show the opposite.

Here's what interests me as an investor:

The opportunity may not be in choosing which country's bonds to buy, but in choosing which maturity offers better compensation for risk.

Credit ratings tell us which countries are risky.

But the spread curve may tell us where the market is mispricing that risk.

The real question: Are these maturity divergences justified by long-term credit risks, or are they relative-value opportunities hiding in plain sight?

items.title: RT Madison Mills: SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take...
items.description_html:
RT Madison Mills
SCOOP: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, including some attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources told Axios.

The findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond, multiple industry and bank executives told Axios.

Several banks are now preparing for worst-case and even “day after” scenarios, including how to rapidly secure or restore customer accounts if things go wrong, the people said.

Several bank executives told Axios they're struggling to distinguish between human users and AI agents. One executive said banks also struggle to determine whether agents are authorized by customers or potentially operating without their permission, more akin to rogue agent behavior.

Read my latest for Axios here: https://www.axios.com/2026/10/22/ai-agents-banks-unauthorized-accounts-access

items.title: RT The Kobeissi Letter: BREAKING: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell -300,000 barrels last week, to 282.7 million barrels, the lowest level si...
items.description_html:
RT The Kobeissi Letter
BREAKING: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) fell -300,000 barrels last week, to 282.7 million barrels, the lowest level since October 1982.

Since March 20th, US oil inventories in the SPR have dropped -132.8 million, or -32%.

We have now seen drawdowns in 29 of the last 30 weeks.

For perspective, oil reserves in the SPR stood at 653.9 million barrels in 2020, or +131% above current levels.

Meanwhile, commercial crude oil stocks excluding the SPR dropped -3.1 million barrels last week, to 412.5 million barrels, the lowest reading since the end of July.

This is also ~3% below the 5-year average for this time of year.

America's oil stockpiles are at critically low levels.

A net-zero target may start as an ESG commitment, but it ultimately succeeds or fails as a capital-allocation decision. As climate disclosures become increasingly tied to financing and risk management, the real question is no longer what companies commit to, but what projects get funded and why. #CareEdge-ESG delves deeper into this.

Key takeaways:
• Climate ambition must clear the test of bankability, where sustainability outcomes and financial viability intersect.
• Global climate finance reached $1.46 trillion in 2022, yet annual investment needs are estimated at $7.4 trillion by 2030, highlighting the scale of the financing challenge.
• Blended finance structures are emerging as a critical tool to mobilise private capital by addressing specific risk, return and liquidity constraints.
• In India, BRSR Core, the RBI’s climate finance directions and a growing GSS+ debt market are strengthening the link between disclosure, financing and accountability.
• Raising green capital is only half the story; proving measurable climate impact is becoming equally important.

Read full Report: https://www.careedgeesg.com/uploads/global-reports/From_ESG_Commitments_to_Climate_Investments.pdf

CareEdge Group | Saikat Roy | Nikunj Dube | Khushal Agarwal

#ClimateFinance #ESG #SustainableFinance #NetZero

items.title: RT V. Ramgopal Rao, Ph.D.: China has announced research grants extending up to 15 years for promising young scientists. Five years initially, with the...
items.description_html:
RT V. Ramgopal Rao, Ph.D.
China has announced research grants extending up to 15 years for promising young scientists. Five years initially, with the possibility of another ten years. An interesting approach. Breakthrough research needs patience, sustained funding and freedom.

India had an excellent initiative in the #Swarnajayanti Fellowships for young scientists below 40. It offered a monthly honorarium and substantial, flexible research funding. The fellowship was highly competitive and became a prestigious recognition in itself.

I was fortunate to receive this fellowship early in my research career. Looking back, I cannot imagine what I would have done without that support.

But there is a larger leadership #lesson here.

The problem with highly selective schemes is that for every person selected, there may be ten others who are disappointed. Some of them will write to the government, question the selection process and create a narrative that something is fundamentally wrong with the scheme. These days, creating a negative narrative against anything good has become remarkably easy.

Governments come under pressure. And when political leaders and senior bureaucrats are surrounded by people who tell them only what they want to hear, even excellent initiatives can become casualties.

This is where #leadership matters.

Our political leaders and top bureaucrats need to occasionally set aside their protocols and meet young faculty members directly in academic institutions. Not just the senior professors, award winners and institutional heads. The youngest faculty often have the most candid things to say about what is working and what is not.

Throughout my academic leadership roles, I have always made it a point to speak with the youngest faculty in departments and maintain an open door policy. Some of my best insights have come from these conversations.

These days, leadership is also about distinguishing genuine #feedback from organised criticism and noise. Otherwise, we will keep dismantling good initiatives simply because a few people are unhappy.

Starting a good scheme requires vision. Sustaining it despite criticism requires courage and conviction.

The country needs to talk to its young #faculty in academic institutions. 🙏
--------
China picks first researchers for 15-year mega grants https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03151-7

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: “Resilient to Higher Rates”? Or Is the Market Simply Hiding the Damage? US 10-year Treasury yields have risen nearly ...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
“Resilient to Higher Rates”? Or Is the Market Simply Hiding the Damage?

US 10-year Treasury yields have risen nearly 100 bps in 2026. Yet Wall Street remains near record highs.

MS raises an important question: At what point do higher interest rates actually become a problem for equities?

The answer isn't as simple as most investors think.

Higher rates aren't necessarily bearish. What matters is WHY they're rising.

If yields rise because economic growth is accelerating, stronger corporate earnings can offset higher borrowing costs.

But if yields rise because inflation is returning or central banks are tightening excessively, the equation changes.

And here's the interesting part.

While headline indices appear resilient:

🔹 Over half the Russell 3000 has experienced a 20%+ drawdown since June.

🔹 US CCC credit spreads have widened 400 bps YTD.

🔹 AI giants continue investing aggressively, while leveraged businesses struggle with financing costs.

The market isn't immune to higher rates. Its strongest companies are simply absorbing the shock better than the weakest.

Indians love to scroll for food –

A typical Zomato customer browses 12 menus and sees 100 food images before ordering

Deepinder Goyal: “Our recent consumer surveys indicate that over 65% of Zomato app opens are exploratory. In such cases, the user does not know what or where to order from.

items.title: RT Alex Imas: New essay in @ForeignAffairs with James Manyika and @elerianm on steps that can be taken to help AI deliver on its economic promise, dra...
items.description_html:
RT Alex Imas
New essay in @ForeignAffairs with James Manyika and @elerianm on steps that can be taken to help AI deliver on its economic promise, drawing on lessons from cooperative game theory as a guide.

Most conversations treat AI as a general-purpose technology (GPT), and some compare it to the Industrial Revolution. But we think it is more than that: it is also a method for creating new inventions, like the microscope or the scientific method. Economist Zvi Griliches famously called such discoveries IMIs--inventions of a method of invention. Seen this way, AI carries the potential of the Industrial Revolution and the Enlightenment combined.

Yet realizing this potential is a coordination problem. Delivering on the promise of AI requires progress not just on furthering its capabilities, but on building out infrastructure, deep adoption across the economy, and buy-in from many different groups. This is unlikely to happen if people do not feel they have a stake in the upside of the technology. Promises of abstract scientific and medical breakthroughs in the future won't change this when anxieties about near-term disruption are running hot.

Rather than treating AI like a zero-sum game, we argue that it is useful to look to cooperative game theory as a guide. Because models, compute, organizational change, and human upskilling are strong complements, AI has the structure of a "convex game": Each group that joins makes everyone else's contributions more valuable. That makes it possible to form stable coalitions of workers, communities, firms, and developers where incentives are aligned and everyone has a stake in the gains.

The cooperative approach will of course not be easy, but we will make the case that coalitions can start small and grow as the mutual gains become tangible. We provide concrete examples of how this can be done in practice and at scale.

Link to essay here: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/guest-pass/redeem/a9cmC65Jei4

RT Reliance Industries Limited
RIL Media Statement

Reliance Industries Limited Chairman and Managing Director Shri Mukesh Ambani and Executive Director Mr Anant Ambani welcomed US Secretary of State Mr Marco Rubio and US Ambassador to India Mr Sergio Gor to Jamnagar, home to the world’s largest refinery. The Honorable visitors were given a tour of the world-class refinery complex, offering a first-hand view of its scale, advanced technology and integrated operations.

Secretary Rubio and Ambassador Gor were also explained Reliance’s New Energy giga-factories, which are currently being commissioned in phases, and the data centres under construction. The tour provided an overview of the company’s investments across energy and digital infrastructure, bringing together its well-established advanced manufacturing and deep-tech capabilities. Shri Mukesh Ambani and Shri Anant Ambani outlined Reliance’s long-term vision for the Jamnagar complex and its development as a centre for deep-tech, innovation and advanced manufacturing.

The visit included wide-ranging discussions on the global energy landscape and opportunities for commercial partnerships across conventional and new energy. The exchange covered reliable and affordable energy supplies, technological advances, resilient supply chains and the investment required to meet growing demand.

Discussions also explored the increasing intersection of energy and digital infrastructure, including the role of dependable power in supporting data centres and the expansion of the digital economy. Shri Mukesh Ambani and Shri Anant Ambani shared their perspectives on opportunities for collaboration with US companies, drawing on complementary strengths in technology, engineering and advanced manufacturing. The interaction provided a constructive opportunity to exchange industry perspectives and explore areas of mutual commercial interest.

We are extremely thankful to Secretary of State and the Ambassador for their esteemed visit.

items.description_html:
RT Mike Bird
Some big personal news: I'm moving to join Works in Progress as executive editor, starting next month. I have been hoping for an opportunity to work with @bswud and @s8mb for more than a decade, and I'm incredibly excited to finally have one.

WIP is expanding on every front right now. We'll soon begin coverage of business and finance, as well as putting out more reported features. To that end, we'll be hiring more writers and reporters in the year to come. I'm planning to remain based in the US to help build out our presence here.

The print edition of WIP has existed for less than 12 months, but sometime in the next week or so we will reach our 10,000th paying print subscriber. It's a group that now includes people who've been at the highest echelons of government and who run the world's biggest public companies. We’re already on track to 3x that number next year. We'll be in store at Barnes & Noble, Hudson News and independent newsagents next week too.

I think WIP is providing something that people are craving from physical media right now: fewer, extremely well-crafted pieces in a beautifully designed form. Issues now feature an amazing group of columnists, including Tyler Cowen, Dan Wang and Stephen Kotkin. Each edition is better than the last.

You'll see us in more and more places next year too. In January, our new weekly documentary films will launch on YouTube. We're expanding into the events space, with a new series in North America. The sky is the limit from here on out.

items.title: RT FBI Cyber Division: Two critical vulnerabilities have been identified in PHP, a widely used programming language that powers websites and web appli...
items.description_html:
RT FBI Cyber Division
Two critical vulnerabilities have been identified in PHP, a widely used programming language that powers websites and web applications. These vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) could allow malicious cyber actors to remotely execute code in PHP core, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

The FBI urges organizations to take the following steps now:

➡️ If an immediate update is not feasible it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.

➡️ Immediately update affected PHP installations following the guidance on http://php.net. Inventory where PHP runs in your environment, prioritizing internet-facing systems and vendor products that bundle PHP.

➡️ Monitor web servers for suspicious activity, including PHP processes unexpectedly launching command shells or downloading files. Ensure appropriate process-monitoring capabilities are in place to help identify potential exploitation.

➡️ If you find signs of compromise, isolate affected systems, preserve your web server and PHP logs, and report it to your local FBI field office or http://www.ic3.gov. Those reports help us identify the actors involved and warn other organizations before they become victims.

For the latest information, follow PHP’s announcement on http://php.net, CERT-EU Security Advisory 2026-018, and CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

You cant revere a river as divine and simultaneously turn her into a landfill.

If this is how we treat the river we claim to worship then maybe we dontt deserve to call her MAA at all.

Period !!

items.title: RT Anuj Singhal अनुज सिंघल: In today’s earnings release, Eternal released a shareholder letter. What caught my eye was Deepinder Goyal’s Ke...
items.description_html:
RT Anuj Singhal अनुज सिंघल
In today’s earnings release, Eternal released a shareholder letter. What caught my eye was Deepinder Goyal’s Key Takeaways on AI http://Dark.ai: A privacy-first AI platform

•Deepinder is developing http://Dark.ai, an AI platform focused on privacy and confidentiality.

•It aims to protect conversations, personal thoughts, research and business ideas.

•The platform will use fine-tuned open-weight models, its own infrastructure and end-to-end encryption.

•Users will control their encrypted memory across sessions.

•It is designed for founders, researchers, scientists, enterprises and governments.

•Deepinder hopes to launch http://Dark.ai globally within 2026.

•He says its AI models will prioritise truth over simply pleasing users.

AI agents: Threat or opportunity for Zomato and Blinkit?
•Zomato and Blinkit face relatively low risk from AI agents, while District faces medium-to-high risk.

•More than 65% of Zomato app opens are exploratory, according to Deepinder. Customers enjoy discovering restaurants, browsing menus and looking at food pictures.

•AI agents may take over repetitive tasks such as repeat orders and restocking, but Deepinder says reordered carts currently account for only a low-single-digit share on Zomato and Blinkit.

•AI can place an order, but fulfilling it reliably is much harder.

•Zomato depends on coordination between restaurants, kitchens, delivery partners, routing and payments.

•Blinkit relies on real-time inventory, dark-store operations, picking and dispatch to enable rapid deliveries.

•Deepinder argues that the company controlling fulfilment and taking responsibility for the customer outcome will retain significant value.

Five important implications for investors
1Execution becomes the moat: Operational excellence and fulfilment infrastructure may matter more than owning the customer interface.

2Markets could consolidate: AI agents may direct customers towards the best-performing platforms, strengthening market leaders.

3Content advantages may weaken: AI can aggregate reviews, ratings and information from across the internet, reducing the value of proprietary content alone.

4New market opportunities could emerge: Strong fulfilment infrastructure may help companies enter categories previously protected by established content advantages.

5AI could generate incremental demand: Personalised recommendations from AI agents may create additional transactions, potentially reducing reliance on traditional customer acquisition channels such as Google and Meta.

What about profitability?
•Deepinder believes AI intermediation need not automatically compress margins for Zomato and Blinkit.

•Platforms that continue to power sales and fulfilment should be able to capture a fair share of the transaction economics.

•However, this is his strategic thesis, not a guarantee that margins will remain unaffected.

The central investment takeaway: Deepinder believes AI may weaken businesses that rely primarily on customer discovery and content, while strengthening companies with superior supply chains, fulfilment capabilities and execution.

India’s agriculture loan book has seen improving asset quality ratios in recent years, but the 2026 monsoon shortfall may test that trend. According to CareEdge Ratings, stress is likely to emerge with a lag, as affected crop loans gradually turn into non-performing assets.

Key takeaways:
• Agriculture has the highest GNPA ratio among major sectors, with a GNPA ratio of 5.11% as of June 2026.
• Around 68% of bank agriculture credit is concentrated in states that received rainfall 20% or more below normal during the 2026 monsoon.
• The agriculture GNPA ratio is expected to rise to 5.3%-5.6% by March 2028, with monsoon-related stress likely becoming more visible through FY28.
• Including restructured loans, stressed agriculture advances could reach 6.0%-6.3% of total agriculture advances by March 2028.
• Loan waivers, rabi crop outcomes, and the extent of restructuring under the natural calamity framework remain critical monitorables.

• Fire premium declines moderated for a second month, signalling that discounting may be beginning to ease.

items.title: RT Caleb: "Why has it taken you nine years, rather than nine months, to deliver this rallying cry for startups?!" I have been wanting to answer a vers...
items.description_html:
RT Caleb
"Why has it taken you nine years, rather than nine months, to deliver this rallying cry for startups?!"

I have been wanting to answer a version of this question in public for some time. I'll also share some insights from building a life for myself in India as a Canadian.

Firstly, @AaryamanVir and I started RuntimeBRT in July of 2025, so we've only really been at this for ~15 months (a short while in the grand scheme). But what we've been able to pull off together has been nine years in the making.

When I first moved to India in 2017, I didn't realise I was moving here properly. It was not supposed to be a permanent move. I didn't know I'd meet the love of my life in India (she's from Mizoram, which is why I live in Aizawl), I didn't know I'd father two wonderful children here, and I certainly could not have predicted the direction my career has taken.

In 2017, I had just dropped out of college. I was studying photography, which is one of the few things in life that has ever really captivated me. Not because I wanted to monetise it — I do not come from a business family and never knew any entrepreneurs growing up — but because it served as a creative outlet through which I was able to explore the world around me.

I quit my professional photography program because I knew if I didn't quit — if I graduated and got a certificate — that I'd probably use that certificate to get a semi-normal job. Doing so would have been the path of least resistance, but I didn't want a normal job. I didn't want a normal life. I was terrified of the boredom that seemed to pervade the careers of so many adult professionals. I intuitively understood that a large majority of people are not satisfied by their careers, and I was deeply determined to avoid falling into that same trap.

I probably would have gravitated towards startups, had I know what a startup was. At the age of 20, I don't think I'd ever heard the word before.

However, the alternative of working a normal job for a normal salary was a life of uncertainty. That was scary too. Very scary. So scary that the fear of not knowing what to do with one's life actually fuels a large part of the postsecondary education industry (in my opinion). Many kids go to college not because they intrinsically want to, but because they don't know what else they'd do. Even if they do have a dream that deviates from the well-trodden path, they may not have enough self-confidence to go all-in on that dream. They're young, inexperienced, and "that's not how the world works kid!"

In spite of my inexperience and uncertainty, I burned the bridge to a degree by dropping out. I wasn't running towards anything in particular. Rather, I was running away from convention. And to a 20-year-old from Canada, India was textbook unconventional. I moved here with my DSLR and a tiny portfolio of photographs. I spent a lot of time doing street photography in and around Delhi. Much of 2017 and early 2018 consisted of me putting myself in uncomfortable social situations with strangers to see if I could capture moments with my camera that felt deeply human.

These street photography outings were where I first fell in love with India and its people. Reinterpreting your note about how picture abhi baaki hai, I have attached some pictures that I took during this chapter of my life.

My photography eventually led me to a wedding in Rajasthan where I was the unofficial photographer. I met my former co-founder at that event. He saw me taking pictures and asked me if I had videography experience too. I told him that I did. That's when he shared one of his dreams with me: he wanted to build a YouTube channel celebrating Indian startups. He wasn't very good with cameras though and needed someone who could help with shoot and editing. I didn't even know what a startup was. I had never heard of Bengaluru. I was totally oblivious to the thriving ecosystem of young people in India who were trying to create value from scratch. But I said yes, and that yes fundamentally altered the trajectory of my life.

We launched that YouTube channel, Backstage with Millionaires, on January 1st of 2019, and spent the next six years growing it to a million subscribers.

I'd like to think that I'm a fairly hardworking, stubborn person. When I put my mind to something, nothing can stop me. Some of you reading this are probably aware of other life stories of mine that prove this point. But building a social media brand to 1M+ followers was, hands down, one of the hardest things I've ever done, and I don't think I would have been able to pull it off without a mission.

Here's what that mission was, and here's how it found me.

Through my videos, I kept meeting young Indian men and women who wanted to build things. They had been told by their parents, teachers, and society at large that "that's not how the world works kid!" But rather than listening to the voice of authority, they had forged an alternative path for themselves by getting into business. "If that's not how the world works, then I'm going to change the world." What audacity! I didn't (and still don't, really) have any business experience, yet I found that these entrepreneurs were just like me! Rebels. Dreamers. Risk takers. Idealists. Hard workers. I was incredibly inspired by their stories. India ain't Canada or the States! Choosing to build here takes guts.

These founders were living life on their own terms. I realised that my mission was to help them actualise their vision in any way I could.

Initially there wasn't much I could do to assist them. We ended 2019 with a very small audience of ~2,000 subscribes. But as the years went on, and as we got better at making content, and as the audience grew, I began to realise that the videos my team and I were making were having a meaningful impact! Founders from the furthest corners of India would reach back out after a video went viral and thank us for helping them to reach investors, hire talent, and sell their products to customers.

I was helping them, in a small way, to change the world. And this work felt very important to me. There is no greater purpose in life (in my opinion) than serving others. It may be the entire point of life, actually.

Starting up is also one of the hardest things you can do. It takes everything to build a business. Everything. It's especially hard in India. Founders face many unique obstacles in this subcontinent that they probably wouldn't need to face elsewhere. Being able to ease that burden a bit by giving them visibility was and is very fulfilling for me.

Aaryaman and I reconnected in early 2025. He and @RahulSanghi1 had been building Tigerfeathers for a couple of years at that point. We shared a mission, even though we had been working in isolation.

We all believe that India's Age of Audacity is upon us. We also believe that the disruptive companies this age is ushering in aren't being talked about enough by India's existing news media industry (who seem laser-focused on politics, conflict, Bollywood gossip, and other TRP-friendly topics).

Aaryaman suggested that by joining forces, we could better-fulfil the duty that the press had failed in. I agreed.

We started @RuntimeBRT in July of 2025 and have grown our audience to ~3 lakh collective followers in 15 months. We don't use gimmicks or growth hacks. We show it how it is. What we have found is that there's a real hunger for candid, informative, dense videos about what's actually happening in Indian tech.

I'm immensely grateful to Aaryaman for his belief, support and vision. As many have said in their replies to your post, he is indeed the goat.

I'm also thankful to you, @anandmahindra, for spotlighting our work at RuntimeBRT and giving oxygen to so many hardworking Indian founders and teams. Your support is invaluable. India needs more people of your stature to take an active role in fostering technological innovation.

Indeed, the picture isn’t over yet! India's Age of Audacity has only just begun, and it's being led by her youth.

RT hari_haran
Re @mercatus was one of the earliest believers in us.

At the time, @naveen_venk and I had no product, no customers and very little money.

We were two twenty-somethings with a thesis: AI could fundamentally change how chips are designed.

Most people did not believe us. But @srajagopalan and emergent ventures did.

Their $15,000 grant allowed us to incorporate @archgen_ , keep building and gain access to the GCP credits we needed to run our early experiments.

That compute helped us develop the optimization system that eventually ranked #1 in the Macro Placement Challenge from @WeAreHRT and Partcl

That first check was more than capital. It gave us time, credibility and the confidence to continue before there was much evidence that we would succeed.

Today, @archgen_ is backed by @ycombinator

We are still pursuing the same belief: chip design can become dramatically faster through AI.

Thank you, @srajagopalan and @tylercowen for believing before it was obvious.

items.title: RT Ananth Rupanagudi: The shadowy veranda of the palace of Maharaja Jatindramohan of the Tagore family, Calcutta, India—1907. Located at Pathuriaghat...
items.description_html:
RT Ananth Rupanagudi
The shadowy veranda of the palace of Maharaja Jatindramohan of the Tagore family, Calcutta, India—1907. Located at Pathuriaghata in North Kolkata, the Tagore Palace is one of Bengal's most structurally unique 19th-century heritage landmarks. Originally built as a traditional mansion, it was later reimagined by Maharaja Bahadur Sir Jatindra Mohan Tagore into a European-style fortress that stood out sharply from traditional Indian architecture.

The site originally housed a grand three-story mansion built by Kali Kumar Tagore (son of Raja Gopi Mohan Tagore). Kali Kumar later handed the property over to his younger brother, Prasanna Coomar Tagore, a legendary legal luminary and a director of Hindu College.

Prasanna Kumar disinherited his own son following a family dispute, passing the property to his nephew, Maharaja Jatindra Mohan Tagore (1831–1908). In 1895, Jatindra Mohan pulled down sections of the old house to build a palace fit for a prince, radically breaking away from standard local architecture.

The palace was a famed center for the arts. Maharaja Jatindra Mohan and his brother Shourendra Mohan Tagore were deep theatre enthusiasts who established the Banga Natyalaya here. Legendary gatherings took place in its halls, including the staging of Kalidas's Malavikagnimitram in July 1859. Historical figures, including Asian and European royalty and the 18th US President General Ulysses S. Grant, visited the premises. #Kolkata #history @somnath1978

RT Javier Blas
MIDDLE EAST FLOWS: Not only flows have proven resilient, but over the last few days (particularly since Oct 16), SoH traffic has surged despite Iranian attacks.

Total Middle East crude flows (ex-Iran, including SoH and all the bypass pipelines and routes) are back to >90% of pre-war levels (last seen in late Sept), and even higher if using a short 7-day average. Refined products flows remain significantly below. Caveat: flows are very uneven, with some days of large number of tanker crossings, followed by very quiet days.

Overall, physical Middle East crude oil premia has continued to drop; just the opposite of what has happened to flat prices. The Oman-Dubai differential has fallen to a 3-month low of ~$4 a barrel. The differential was >$30 a barrel in mid-Sept.

items.title: Engineered Goods exports from India India’s engineering exports grew 20% in H1 FY27 to $70.9 bn. EEPC now expects a record $150 bn this year. Why the...
items.description_html:
Engineered Goods exports from India

India’s engineering exports grew 20% in H1 FY27 to $70.9 bn. EEPC now expects a record $150 bn this year.

Why the sudden jump? 5 reasons:

1. Metals boom. The Iran war shut the Strait of Hormuz and knocked out Gulf aluminium, about 8% of world supply. Prices hit a 4-year high. India’s aluminium exports jumped 49% in May, and steel exports 51% in July.

2. US tariff reset. Washington cut tariffs on Indian goods from 50% to 18% in February. Shipments to the US were up 20% in July.

3. China is buying. Engineering exports to China rose 82% in April and 74% in June.

4. A new door into West Asia. With routes to the UAE and Saudi blocked, exports to Oman more than quadrupled in June.

5. The UK trade deal is live. It kicked in on 15 July, and UK shipments were already up 34% in the first two months of the year.

items.title: RT Michael Pettis: FT: In Brazil, "almost 2mn people, mostly men, now work full-time for transport or delivery apps — around 2 per cent of the workfo...
items.description_html:
RT Michael Pettis
FT: In Brazil, "almost 2mn people, mostly men, now work full-time for transport or delivery apps — around 2 per cent of the workforce — with driver numbers climbing 37 per cent in three years, according to government research. The most common reason people work for the apps is that they could not find another job."

The FT notes that in Brazil, the transport and delivery app economy has become a kind of unemployment insurance scheme, although one with declining "benefits".

The same is true in China. It is hard to get good data, but the best estimates are that 12% of China's working population works in the gig economy, of which 7% work in the transport and delivery app economy – i.e. three to four times the share in Brazil.
https://www.ft.com/content/3868b320-2c24-418e-b702-c86e2620e4a6

items.title: RT Nithin Kamath: The ED just froze trading accounts holding about ₹200 crore in an alleged WhatsApp-driven pump and dump involving two listed compan...
items.description_html:
RT Nithin Kamath
The ED just froze trading accounts holding about ₹200 crore in an alleged WhatsApp-driven pump and dump involving two listed companies.

It's crazy that even in 2026, people still fall for stock tips on WhatsApp, Telegram, SMS, and social media. This is probably the silliest way to lose money.

Given how late in the cycle we are, these instances are only going to increase. We're already seeing more pump and dumps, whether through WhatsApp groups or influencers peddling IPOs and stocks. This won't end well.

So the next time you get a message promising easy money, just ask Claude or ChatGPT whether it's a good idea. It could save you a lot of money.

It's become a cliché, but nowhere is "if it's too good to be true, it probably is" truer than in the stock market.

items.title: RT Prasanna Viswanathan: China announces export controls for tunnel boring machines (TBMs) From Nov 18, exporting TBMs will require a licence. These a...
items.description_html:
RT Prasanna Viswanathan
China announces export controls for tunnel boring machines (TBMs)

From Nov 18, exporting TBMs will require a licence. These are the machines fuelling India’s infrastructurebooming especially metros and highway tunnels.

Beijing is classifying them as “dual-use” items, which gives the move a security label, but in effect it is economic coercion.

This has happened before. In 2024, China began delaying customs clearances for TBM shipments to India, and in August 2025 it told India it had lifted the curbs on TBMs. With this licence rule, the delays become a formal mechanism that Beijing can tighten or loosen whenever relations change.

India’s dependence here is real, but it is narrower than it might look. TBM imports from China had already dropped sharply, from $18 million in 2022-23 to $3 million in 2023-24, and most self-propelled TBMs have come from outside China. The serious risk is deayed metro timelines and cost escalation if suppliers’ Chinese plants or components get stuck in licensing.

India’s response has to be to make these machines itself, and that work has started. The government is preparing a $1.2 billion incentive scheme to make tunnel boring machines, firefighting equipment and elevators in India. It is expected to bring in about $1.8 billion in investment over seven years.

BEML is preparing to manufacture TBMs locally, and L&T could also benefit. Building this capacity will take years, but each round of export controls from China makes the case for it stronger. https://asia.nikkei.com/economy/china-announces-export-controls-for-tunnel-boring-machines

items.title: NYT: "Surging exports and the industrial production needed to sustain them kept China’s economy growing over the past three months, even as consumer ...
items.description_html:
NYT: "Surging exports and the industrial production needed to sustain them kept China’s economy growing over the past three months, even as consumer spending stagnated and investment plunged. The result is an economy increasingly dependent on selling goods abroad, even as domestic demand deteriorates."

NYT's Keith Bradsher gets this right. Many other analysts have been presenting this year's economic data as describing a two-track economy, with a sluggish domestic economy being balanced by a brilliant export economy.

But that is a very poor description of what is actually happening. Yes, net exports are surging, but this isn't a sign of a viable export sector. If the export sector were very profitable, it might make sense to describe it this way, but exports aren't especially profitable except in relation to domestic sales, where except in a few sectors businesses are struggling to make any profit at all, and once direct and indirect subsidies are backed out, much of China's exports are net value destroyers for the economy, with the losses capitalized on balance sheets in the form of surging debt.

When an economy produces far more than it can absorb through domestic consumption or investment, it must either export the balance or close down domestic production. Given how high real unemployment is, especially among the young, Beijing has no choice but to force the former, even if this comes at an economic cost.

The surge in China's net exports, in other words, is not a sigh of a strong and profitable export sector. If it takes rising debt, continued subsidies, and growing exports in order to prevent a contraction in domestic production, the surge in net exports is simply another way of describing weak domestic demand.

Surging exports are usually a good sign for an economy. Surging net exports usually are not.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/18/business/china-economy-gdp.html?smid=tw-share

items.title: None of the data that came out today gives us a different picture of the Chinese economy from what we’ve seen all year. The economy is still heavily ...
items.description_html:
None of the data that came out today gives us a different picture of the Chinese economy from what we’ve seen all year. The economy is still heavily focused on boosting production and is still struggling with boosting demand.

GDP grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, slightly higher than expected, from 5.0% in the first quarter and 4.3% in the second quarter. Year to date GDP has grown 4.6%, just above the bottom of the GDP growth target for 2026.

In September, industrial output went up by 5.5% year on year, or 5.3% for the first nine months. Meanwhile retail sales increased by 1.1% in September, or 2.6% for the first nine months.

The gap between domestic production and domestic consumption, in other words, continues to widen rather than narrow, with the gap much wider in September than it has been over the rest of the year. This can only be balanced by rising investment or a rising trade surplus.

And it clearly isn’t being balanced by rising investment. Fixed asset investment in the first nine months of 2026 was down 7.2% year on year, or 4.2% with property investment deducted.

The decline in overall investment was driven by an even sharper decline in private investment, which was down by 10.4% year on year, or 6.7% with property investment deducted. Disaggregated by sector, investment in infrastructure declined by 4.2% year on year, manufacturing by 2.1%, and real estate development by 20.6%. The good news is that the decline in investment may finally be bottoming out, with fixed asset investment in September, rising by 0.07% month on month.

We will probably see fiscal expansion in the last quarter of this year, although I think it would be a good thing if Beijing let growth come in at the bottom of the target, especially if they lower the target further in 2027. Debt is simply growing too fast, and it is growing fast only because of the urgent desire to meet politically-determined GDP growth targets. The longer this goes on, the more difficult the ultimate adjustment will be.

items.title: RT Press Trust of India: VIDEO | Delhi: Reacting to the judicial custody of CJP co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, CJP legal head Ratna Singh...
items.description_html:
RT Press Trust of India
VIDEO | Delhi: Reacting to the judicial custody of CJP co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, CJP legal head Ratna Singh says, "We have been here since morning. We were told that the entire hearing would take place at 12.00 pm. Today, everything was complete, the verification was done, and all requirements were met. We have been waiting here since noon. The SEM (Special Executive Magistrate) was at the police station by 1:30 pm, but he did not enter the courtroom until 5.00 pm. When he finally arrived, he refused to hear our case on its merits regarding whether Saurav and Ashutosh should be released from judicial custody. Instead, he made arbitrary remarks. The public prosecutor, who had not appeared at the police station for the last four days, was present today. Within about five minutes of the proceedings, the SEM told the court that he had received a threatening message. From that point on, the entire discussion revolved solely around that message. It is clear that this entire episode was orchestrated. They had decided beforehand to come into the courtroom and focus exclusively on this alleged threatening message, completely bypassing whether the formalities required for Saurav and Ashutosh's release were fulfilled. Given how this process has been deliberately delayed and handled, I am utterly disappointed..."

items.title: RT Roger E. A. Farmer: That’s a question for the philosophy of science. My friend Axel Leijonhufvud had a metaphor of science as a tree with many bra...
items.description_html:
RT Roger E. A. Farmer
That’s a question for the philosophy of science. My friend Axel Leijonhufvud had a metaphor of science as a tree with many branches. Each branch represents an alternative possible path along which the subject might progress.

In the experimental sciences, false approaches are quickly discovered by experiment and those branches are trimmed. Progress appears linear.

In non experimental sciences the discipline can adopt approaches that are ultimately shown to be false but which persist for long periods of time. Ultimately it takes a large natural experiment like the Great Depression or the Stagflation of the 1970s to cause a course correction.

In the period between natural experiments, when multiple theories appear equally viable, the science is governed by gatekeepers who edit top journals and are educated at a small group of elite institutions. These gatekeepers provide a filter on acceptable discourse. This institutional structure has its benefits since, if it is difficult to empirically distinguish alternative theories, it would be highly disruptive if every fresh graduate student were to branch out in an entirely new direction. But the filtering out of new ideas can also cause the exiting corpus of thought to become sclerotic.

Influential schools of thought, like NK economics, are practiced by generations of students who acquire human capital and have an incentive not to rock the boat. Prestigious awards like the Nobel Prize and the John Bates Clarke Award provide incentives to color within the lines and these incentives are strongest when widely recognized deserving recipients have not yet been recognized. Elite universities maintain active offices whose goal is to lobby the Nobel committee on behalf of their own professoriate.

I have never met a brilliant young academic who did not aspire to be recognized as a Nobel Laureate: Through that mechanism prestigious awards offer important incentives to scientific excellence. But the prizes themselves also act as brakes on progress since a major course correction in the direction of the discipline would depreciate, overnight, the accumulated capital of generations of scholars.

In the words of Max Planck: “Progress occurs one funeral at a time.”

For further reading on these ideas I recommend Lakatos’ essay in in ‘Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge’ https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/criticism-and-the-growth-of-knowledge/74C4E5A7D52C5D11F65849CCD0710012

items.title: Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend? Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm....
items.description_html:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm. A hacker, a scammer, a disgruntled employee. So we build walls, filters and permissions to keep bad intentions out.

That assumption may be becoming outdated. The bigger danger with AI agents may not be an agent that wants to cause harm, but one that is too determined to do exactly what it was told.

Consider this as an example: agents were given a legitimate task: complete a cybersecurity test. When the obvious route was blocked, they found another way. They escaped their sandbox, retrieved passwords and gained access they were not supposed to have. Nobody told them to attack anything. They were simply doing their job and did not care how they got it done.

Think of telling a friend: “Get me a coffee, whatever it takes.” A normal person understands the implicit boundaries. “Whatever it takes” does not mean robbing the café. An AI agent may not automatically understand those boundaries. It isn't evil. It is obedient without necessarily possessing common sense about where the objective should stop.

This is where the tail risk becomes interesting. We tend to prepare for risks based on what we expect an adversary to do. But a sufficiently capable system can create a serious problem without any malicious intent at all. It only needs a strong objective, enough capability and insufficient constraints.

And AI agents dramatically increase the number of entities that can act inside a digital environment. More agents, more autonomy, more permissions, more connections and more opportunities for unintended behaviour.

The attack surface is no longer just humans trying to break into systems. It increasingly includes machines acting inside them.

We were guarding the door against the burglar. The unexpected risk may come from the helper we willingly let inside.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable thought is this:

The dangerous AI agent may not be the one that refuses to follow instructions. It may be the one that follows them perfectly.

Most AI in security today is a general-purpose model with a security prompt on top. It was trained on internet text, it looks at one alert at a time, and it can write a confident root cause that the evidence doesn’t support.

items.title: RT Nandakishor m: Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sou...
items.description_html:
RT Nandakishor m
Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sourcing a new physics-based typed decision model called Vega.
The interesting parts. It is only 800 million parameters (4B is also there), with 73k token support, image support, and surpassing many of the jev benchmarks in single-shot. Implemented an engine+adapter as a Test-Time Training Architecture.
Imagine you are giving input to the model like "ignore all previous conversations," which is called the observation, along with a question, "Is this trying to override the instructions of the model?" and your possible outcomes are YES or NO. The whole prompt is passed to an LLM/VLM (yeah, image-supported), then from the hidden layers, we can extract the observation, question, the yes and no, and last token. These will be vectors, and we can project it by multiplying with wieghts; then, first, using the observation projection, we can create a landscape with valleys; then, using the question and last-token vectors, we can initialise a ball in the valley, and using YES or NO, we can get the candidate location of the ball. Depends on the number of outcomes we create valleys; that is, here YES and NO, so 2. When the ball fall on YES valley, we get the answer. There is friction also influencing how the ball moves.
TLDR: It's like creating valleys of outcomes that we need and throwing a ball that will slow down based on friction and settle on the best outcome
Blog: https://www.nandakishorm.com/writing/vega
GitHub: https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/vegaml

items.title: Telecom networks are evolving from connectivity infra into distributed sensing infra that's critical for national security. The legacy infra primarily...
items.description_html:
Telecom networks are evolving from connectivity infra into distributed sensing infra that's critical for national security. The legacy infra primarily connects a phone, vehical or a device to the network. ISAC turns telco infra into a wide area sensing network to detect, tract objects, including drones without needing a dedicated radar at every sensing location. This is such a critical part of the security sovereignty. For existing telcos, this means, theycan offer sensing services using same infra. A potential new revenue stream.

In AI native physical world, radio networks could become sources of realtime information about moving objects & their surroundings. Combine this with AI, you can support traffic optimization, industrial monitoring, infra/public protection.

If India can develop, deploy sophisticated sensing enabled telco infra, we gain the capabilities that go beyond simply buying connectivity from a foreign stellite provider who can cut us off in ever changing geopolitical situation.

Eventually, everything is down to who controls the network and the data? Market access cannot be isolated from national security. It's all about who gets a strategic control over the next layer of digital infra.

items.title: RT Prasanna Tantri: To appreciate the Indian government’s caution on Starlink, I strongly recommend Edward Fishman’s New York Times bestseller, Chok...
items.description_html:
RT Prasanna Tantri
To appreciate the Indian government’s caution on Starlink, I strongly recommend Edward Fishman’s New York Times bestseller, Chokepoints. It shows how America turned its dominance in finance and technology into instruments of state policy.

Private ownership offers no insulation from state power. The restrictions on Huawei and ZTE illustrate how dependence on American technology can become a source of geopolitical vulnerability. Under the Foreign Direct Product Rule, even companies outside America needed US permission to supply Huawei with certain products made using American technology. Washington’s reach extended far beyond American firms and borders.

India should take that lesson seriously. Greater dependence on foreign-controlled critical infrastructure creates the risk that commercial access will eventually become conditional on political compliance.

Economic interdependence can deliver prosperity. But in periods of geopolitical conflict, it can also constrain a country’s freedom to make its own choices. Short-term commercial gains must be weighed against that loss of autonomy.

India is right to insist on security safeguards for Starlink. Economic sovereignty is difficult to recover once critical dependencies are entrenched.
